lesson_title: State Actors: North Korea in Depth

metadata.note: No assigned reading for this lesson; every question is grounded in a visible slide.

lectures.title: State Actors: North Korea in Depth - lesson synthesis

questions.question_stem: An agent asks which state carried out a large theft. Who answers that, in the lesson's view?
questions.correct_answer: The government; for Bybit the FBI named North Korea, and the analyst quotes it.
incorrect_answers: The analyst, who reads the state from the pattern of the trace alone and states it.
The analytics firm whose report was published first, since firms are first to see it.
No one can say, because a theft by a state is outside the scope of any report.
questions.explanation: The analyst characterizes what moved and quotes the government's attribution with its source and date; the analyst does not attribute a state from the chain alone.

questions.question_stem: Which control points does the United States act at, according to the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: OFAC designations and issuer freezes, such as $344M in USDT frozen with OFAC in April 2026.
incorrect_answers: Mining pools and validator nodes, which it orders to reject a state's blocks outright.
Wallet software makers, which it orders to disable accounts used by sanctioned states at once.
Block explorers, which it orders to hide the addresses of a state actor from public view.
questions.explanation: The table on blockchain cutting both ways lists OFAC designations and issuer freezes as the United States' control points.

questions.question_stem: As of December 2025, what did Chainalysis report about North Korea's 2025 thefts?
questions.correct_answer: At least $2.02B, about 59% of all stolen worldwide, from 74% fewer known attacks.
incorrect_answers: At least $2.02B, about 59% of all stolen worldwide, from many more attacks than 2024.
About $660M, about 59% of all stolen worldwide, from 20 incidents in the year.
At least $1.34B, about 12% of all stolen worldwide, from 47 incidents in the year.
questions.explanation: The 2025 row reads: at least $2.02B, about 59% of over $3.4B stolen worldwide, and 74% fewer known attacks (Chainalysis, 18 December 2025).
questions.lesson_block: North Korea's thefts: fewer, larger, more in 2025

specific_source.anchor: North Korea's thefts: fewer, larger, more in 2025

questions.question_stem: What is the right way to use a name such as TraderTraitor in a report?
questions.correct_answer: Quote the name with the agency and the date, here the FBI on 26 February 2025.
incorrect_answers: Coin a label from the trace if the pattern fits the case, then use it in your report.
Use it as your own label for the cluster you traced in the case, and add no source.
Treat it as a firm's product name, not a government one, and skip the date.
questions.explanation: Lazarus Group, APT38 and TraderTraitor are names the FBI and Treasury use. Quote the name, the agency and the date; never coin one from a trace.

specific_source.anchor: The names come from the government

questions.question_stem: How did the Bybit thieves get the signers to approve the transaction?
questions.correct_answer: They changed the web page the signers used, so the signers approved an altered call.
incorrect_answers: They broke Bybit's contract itself so no signer was needed for the transfer.
They guessed the signers' private keys after many tries and signed in their place instead.
They bribed a Bybit insider who then approved the transfer in the signers' stead.
questions.explanation: The thieves did not break Bybit's contract or Bybit's systems. Malicious JavaScript on Safe{Wallet}'s bucket altered the transaction the signers' browsers loaded.
questions.lesson_block: Bybit: the way in was a wallet's website, not the contract

specific_source.anchor: Bybit: the way in was a wallet's website, not the contract

questions.question_stem: In the five steps of the Bybit theft, which step is seen on chain?
questions.correct_answer: The cold wallet delegatecalled a contract that rewrote its masterCopy.
incorrect_answers: A developer's machine at Safe{Wallet} was hacked before the theft.
Malicious JavaScript was placed in the AWS S3 bucket two days before.
Clean files replaced the malicious ones about two minutes afterward.
questions.explanation: Only step 4 is seen on chain, which the day 8 lab walks through; steps 1, 2, 3 and 5 happened off chain.

questions.question_stem: In the first minutes after Bybit, the thieves swapped tokens such as stETH for ETH. Why?
questions.correct_answer: No issuer can freeze ETH, unlike the tokens an issuer could freeze.
incorrect_answers: ETH is easier to hide because it is a privacy coin with hidden values.
ETH has no fees, so the thieves could split the funds across addresses.
ETH is accepted by every exchange without any identity checks at all.
questions.explanation: The 'Why' column says no issuer can freeze ETH. Stolen stETH, cmETH and other tokens were swapped for ETH on DEXs in the first minutes.
questions.lesson_block: Bybit: out of freezable tokens first, then to Bitcoin

specific_source.anchor: Bybit: out of freezable tokens first, then to Bitcoin

questions.question_stem: What laundering shape repeats across North Korea's cases from 2022 to 2026?
questions.correct_answer: Mix or swap, cross chains, then cash out; the service changes when one is sanctioned or shut.
incorrect_answers: Hold the funds in the thief's wallet for years until attention fades, then cash out.
Send every theft straight to one exchange account until that account is frozen in the end.
Spend the funds on goods on chain, so nothing ever has to be turned back into cash again.
questions.explanation: The lesson's table runs Ronin, Harmony, Sinbad, the 2024 UN figure, Bybit and Drift. When a service is sanctioned or shut, the next case uses another.

questions.question_stem: What did the durable nonce accounts that the Drift attacker created allow?
questions.correct_answer: Signers' approvals could be sent later, so pre-signed transactions waited to be used.
incorrect_answers: The attacker could hide the stolen tokens in a separate Solana account until the theft.
The attacker could swap the stolen tokens at a rate that was fixed well before the theft.
The attacker could freeze the protocol's withdrawals for a day before the theft began.
questions.explanation: Durable nonce accounts were created 23 to 30 March 2026, 'used so that signers' approvals could be sent later'. Two of five Security Council signers pre-signed transactions that hid admin actions.

questions.question_stem: Which detail TRM reported for Drift is a behavior many thieves share, not a mark of one actor?
questions.correct_answer: Staging began with 10 ETH from Tornado Cash, which many thieves use.
incorrect_answers: ETH first moved around 09:00 Pyongyang time, which is a timing line only.
Laundering was faster than Bybit's, which was an attributed case.
Most funds bridged to Ethereum within hours, which is a unique mark of it.
questions.explanation: The table pairs each TRM detail with the kind of line it is. Tornado Cash use is behavior; the Pyongyang time is timing.
questions.lesson_block: Drift: a firm's assessment is not a government attribution

specific_source.anchor: Drift: a firm's assessment is not a government attribution

questions.question_stem: How did Elliptic describe the Drift attack?
questions.correct_answer: As a 'suspected' DPRK-linked attack, its indicators 'consistent with' past DPRK operations.
incorrect_answers: As confirmed North Korean, since the FBI had named the actor by the same date in a public statement.
As a criminal gang's theft with no DPRK link, because the funds went on to Ethereum.
As an insider theft at Drift, since two of five signers had approved the transactions.
questions.explanation: Elliptic called it 'suspected', its indicators 'consistent with' past DPRK-attributed operations, and it reports no government attribution.

questions.question_stem: Which statement belongs in the lesson's 'Say' column?
questions.correct_answer: Address X received $Y from the Bybit theft addresses the FBI listed on 26 Feb 2025.
incorrect_answers: The service that took the funds violated sanctions, as the trace made plain.
The user who received the funds is a North Korean agent working for the state.
The funds will be frozen, because the issuer can freeze this token at any time.
questions.explanation: Report exposure with the designation or attribution and its date; whether it broke a sanction is not the analyst's call.

questions.question_stem: It is 2 April 2026, an agent asks 'Was it North Korea?' about Drift, and no government has spoken. What form should the answer take?
questions.correct_answer: Quote TRM's assessment with its date as the firm's view, then give your own confidence word.
incorrect_answers: Say North Korea did it, since the trace matches Bybit closely and TRM agrees with that view, too.
Say nothing about North Korea until a government names the actor in writing, then repeat that name.
Say it is confirmed at High confidence, since two firms agree with each other on the whole matter.
questions.explanation: The practice slide's model answer is 'TRM assesses (April 2026) that North Korea likely carried out the Drift theft', then your own confidence.
